title: Evaluate rural schemes

blocks.heading: Evaluate rural schemes
blocks.text: Rural schemes should address a specified livelihood or service barrier with feasible resources and participation. Production obstacles stop growing or making output; marketing obstacles prevent reaching buyers or obtaining sales. A loan for seed will not repair a blocked selling route.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Credit and small projects
blocks.text: Credit makes resources available now with repayment obligations; a small project may fit local skills and manageable demand. It can remove a finance bottleneck, but repayment timing, borrowing cost and uncertain returns matter. Debt cannot by itself create water, markets or viable yields.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Farmers’ cooperatives
blocks.text: A cooperative is owned and operated jointly by members to meet shared economic or social needs. Pooling storage, purchases or marketing can improve access and bargaining, but requires agreed contributions, transparent decisions and workable coordination.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Resettlement
blocks.text: Resettlement relocates people or productive access to another area under an organised scheme. Land alone is insufficient: water, services, livelihoods, consent and continuing support matter. Moving people to unsuitable land can replace one access problem with another.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Integrated development
blocks.text: Integrated rural development links related needs such as roads, water, skills, health and market access rather than treating them in isolation. Community mobilisation can coordinate local knowledge and effort. Complex coordination and maintenance responsibilities can impede implementation if resources and roles are unclear.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Grassroots development
blocks.text: Grassroots development is initiated with active participation by local people around their priorities and resources, rather than solely directed from above. Local knowledge can improve relevance and ownership; unequal voice, limited funding or excluded groups can undermine those benefits. Participation needs influence, not attendance alone.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Appropriate farming methods
blocks.text: Appropriate farming methods fit the soil, water, task, skills, costs and environmental conditions. A method that conserves soil but cannot be maintained may fail in practice. Judge useful output and long-term resource condition together rather than choosing by complexity alone.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Match the scheme
blocks.text: An invented cooperative can either fund shared grading equipment or offer members a larger fertiliser loan. Buyers already accept the crop, but inconsistent grading causes price deductions. Grading equipment addresses that observed marketing problem; fertiliser could raise production but does not correct the deductions. Compare the equipment’s maintenance costs and the expected avoided losses before choosing. A scheme should fit the diagnosed constraint.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Several benefits and obstacles of rural schemes
blocks.text: A farmers’ cooperative can lower input prices through joint purchasing, share transport costs, provide storage, pool marketing and bargaining, connect members to credit and exchange farming advice. These are distinct benefits; repeating “cheaper” for every point hides the mechanism. Members need fair rules, trustworthy records and arrangements for conflicting interests. Loans can finance seed or tools before sales generate cash, but repayment costs and a poor harvest can threaten affordability. Resettlement can widen land access yet fail without water, services, productive skills and buyers. An integrated scheme can coordinate these complementary needs but needs clear budgets and agency responsibilities. Grassroots schemes can use local knowledge and voluntary effort, while limited finance and unequal voice can restrict them. Marketing problems include unreliable transport, inadequate storage, poor market information and failure to meet buyer quality requirements; rainfall and soil quality are production problems instead.
context_tags: Codex repair after independent review; original teaching synthesis

blocks.heading: Southern African applications
blocks.text: Land reform and resettlement are Southern African approaches to unequal land access, including in Namibia. Evaluate land suitability and continuing support rather than equating allocated hectares with better livelihoods. Collective farming shares productive work or assets; a cooperative may instead market members’ separately produced crops. Small self-help projects can pool labour around a local need. An integrated rural scheme connects farming support with roads, water or other services. Use these named approaches to describe how rural development is attempted in the region; their names do not establish that every scheme succeeded.
